prompt: In AWS's February 28, 2017 S3 postmortem, the index and placement subsystems required a full, multi-hour restart to recover instead of a fast failover. What does that recovery time imply about the architecture?
choices: There was no fast, warm, incremental recovery path for a fleet-wide capacity loss of that size -- only a slow, cold, integrity-verified rebuild
S3 intentionally throttles recovery speed to avoid overloading customers with sudden availability
The restart was slow purely because of unrelated network congestion that day
Nothing can be inferred about recovery mechanisms from restart duration alone

prompt: During the same 2017 S3 outage, why was AWS's own Service Health Dashboard slow to reflect the problem?
choices: AWS employees were on vacation and nobody was available to update it
The dashboard's own backing infrastructure depended on resources in the very region that was impacted -- a circular dependency
The dashboard was hosted by a separate third-party vendor unrelated to AWS
AWS deliberately delays dashboard updates for 24 hours after any incident

prompt: What actually triggered Fastly's June 8, 2021 global outage?
choices: A distributed denial-of-service attack against Fastly's edge network
A scheduled maintenance window that was run without approval
A single customer's valid, policy-compliant configuration change that triggered a latent software bug deployed about a month earlier
A fiber cut affecting Fastly's primary data center

prompt: Why did the Fastly outage take down sites with no business relationship to each other or to the customer who made the triggering change?
choices: All affected sites happened to deploy a bad update on the exact same day by coincidence
They all shared the same unrelated DNS registrar, which failed independently

They were all tenants on the same shared edge fleet, so a fleet-wide software bug became a single point of failure for every tenant behind it, regardless of how unrelated the tenants were to each other
Fastly intentionally took those specific customers offline during the incident

prompt: What is the core idea behind 'shuffle sharding' as a blast-radius containment technique?
choices: Give every tenant the exact same full set of workers so load is always perfectly even
Assign each tenant a small, pseudo-randomly chosen subset of available cells/workers, so any two tenants overlap on only a thin slice of shared infrastructure
Randomly reboot workers on a fixed schedule regardless of tenant assignment
Shard tenants purely alphabetically by name across a fixed number of servers

prompt: In an Istio DestinationRule, which field implements a circuit breaker that ejects an unhealthy backend from the load-balancing pool before its failures cascade to every caller?
choices: trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.simple
trafficPolicy.outlierDetection
subsets.labels
http.route.weight

prompt: The AWS Kinesis disruption of November 25, 2020 cascaded into authentication failures and delayed metrics for services like Cognito and CloudWatch. What does that reveal about those services' architecture?
choices: Cognito and CloudWatch are entirely independent systems with no shared infrastructure, and the cascading failure was coincidental
Cognito and CloudWatch publicly advertised Kinesis as a core dependency well before the incident
They had an internal dependency on Kinesis that was not obvious from outside the provider's own organization, which the failure narrative exposed
The outage only affected Kinesis's own customer-facing API and nothing else

prompt: When judging whether a postmortem's remediation actually bounds future blast radius, what is the key distinction to look for?
choices: Whether the postmortem is longer than 2,000 words

Whether the remediation is an enforced ceiling expressed as a number in a system (a cap, a partition, a quota) versus just added monitoring or alerting that tells a human faster without stopping the failure mode
Whether the company issued a public apology alongside the postmortem
Whether the postmortem names the specific engineer responsible
